editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech is less a devolution offer than a rewriting of the Union argument. For a generation, deindustrialisation in Scotland was told as a national grievance: decisions taken in London by people who did not have to live with them. Burnham accepts that story in full. He calls Ravenscraig's closure a choice made 'hundreds of miles away', and says he reached 'the same conclusion that Scotland had reached'. He then redraws its map, setting Leigh beside Motherwell and Dundee beside Edinburgh.

If the problem is centre against place rather than England against Scotland, then Holyrood can be part of the problem too. That is why the speech dwells on gaps inside Scotland: transport, high streets, Inverclyde's shrinking workforce, seven years of life expectancy across ten miles. It is a pro-Union argument that never mentions the Union, and it gives the Scottish Government little room to refuse without appearing to defend its own centralisation.

The concrete test is the DWP offer. Employment support is one of the few levers of the welfare state still held at Westminster. Parts of it were already handed over after the 2014 referendum, and Scotland ran its own employability programmes. Offering more, on condition that it be pushed down to regions on the 'Easterhouse principle', attaches strings to a transfer of power. Whether Holyrood takes it on those terms will show whether this is partnership or leverage.

There is a quieter tension across this week's announcements. The Prime Minister praises his own record of paying more to have Greater Manchester's buses built in Falkirk. He wants all public procurement run that way, and he promises GBR trains built in Britain. At the same time he is seeking a closer trading relationship with Europe. Deliberately favouring domestic suppliers sits awkwardly with the procurement rules that come with deeper market access. Reindustrialisation by purchasing choice and an EU reset will eventually have to be reconciled.

Both stories also turn on the same buried statistic of youth disconnection. Around one in six young Scots are not in education, employment or training, while under 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. The supply of disengaged young people and the industries' ageing workforces are two sides of one failure of the training pipeline. Small apprenticeship cohorts and new defence colleges will not close that gap on their own.
